quote: The ensuing end-game is clearly in White's favour …
source: Alekhine, My Best Games of Chess 1908–1923 (1927), Game 78, note to Black's 20th move

quote: Black has a Rook and two pawns for two minor pieces, a slight advantage for the end-game, but as yet there is no thought of an end-game.
source: Edward Lasker, Chess Strategy (1915), Game No. 17, note after 14. KxB (Diag. 125)

quote: The following middle game from a match of two masters furnishes an example. After White's seventh move the position of Diagram 49 was reached, in which Black continued with [...b5] with the view to playing [...Bg4] and [...Nd4].
source: Edward Lasker, Chess and Checkers: The Way to Mastership (1918), The Middle Game, Diagram 49
note: Lasker already calls this a middle game; the rule still says opening, since 14 pieces besides kings and pawns remain, both back ranks hold five and the armies have not met.

game: Capablanca's Four Knights model line, as in Capablanca – Lasker, St Petersburg 1914
quote: A very powerful move, which brings us to the middle-game stage, as there is already in view a combination to win quickly by [Nd5].
source: Capablanca, Chess Fundamentals (1921), ch. 6 General strategy of the opening, Example 17, note to 7. B - Kt 5
note: For Capablanca the middle game starts when a concrete combination appears; the rule waits for exchanges, emptied back ranks or interpenetrating armies.

quote: Position after Black's 16th move.
source: Alekhine, My Best Games of Chess 1908–1923 (1927), Game 59, diagram caption

quote: Position after White's 23rd move.
source: Alekhine, My Best Games of Chess 1908–1923 (1927), Game 60, diagram caption

note: Cannot happen: the side to move is read from the position the author annotates.
Cannot happen: the side to move is read from the position the author annotates.

quote: Black has come out of the opening with a Pawn to the good.
source: Capablanca, Chess Fundamentals (1921), Game 6 (Rice Memorial Tournament, 1916), note after Black's 14th move

quote: White is under the impression that he has the better game, because he is a Pawn ahead, but that is not so.
source: Capablanca, Chess Fundamentals (1921), Game 14, note to White's 21st move

quote: As far as the material is concerned the players are about even, as the Queen is worth as much as the two Rooks while Knight and Bishop are an approximate equivalent of the Black Rook and the Pawn which Black is ahead.
source: Edward Lasker, Chess and Checkers: The Way to Mastership (1918), ch. How the different men cooperate, Diagram 30
note: Lasker values two rooks as one queen; the 1-3-3-5-9 scale makes them a pawn more, so the rule reads White a pawn up.

quote: Although three minor pieces are generally an equivalent for the Queen, in this case the White game collapses quickly.
source: Edward Lasker, Chess Strategy (1915), Game No. 30, note to White's 24th move

quote: Besides, the Bishop is better with Rooks than the Knight (see pages 48-56, where the relative values of the Knight and Bishop are compared), and, as already stated, with Pawns on both sides of the board the Bishop is superior because of its long range.
source: Capablanca, Chess Fundamentals (1921), Game 14, note to White's 21st move

quote: Now Black has undoubtedly the better game, with his two Bishops and his strongly-posted Knight in the centre.
source: Alekhine, My Best Games of Chess 1908–1923 (1927), Game 96, note to Black's 9th move

quote: The loss of the present game by Black can be attributed to the fact that his Knights lack bases in the centre, and that in positions of this character the possession of the two Bishops constitutes a decisive advantage for the opponent.
source: Alekhine, My Best Games of Chess 1908–1923 (1927), Game 90 (match, Berlin 1921), note to White's 17th move

quote: On the other hand, the advantage of the two Bishops is illusory, for it is clear that after [...Bf6] White cannot avoid the exchange of his [d4 bishop].
source: Alekhine, My Best Games of Chess 1908–1923 (1927), Game 99 (first match game, Paris 1923), note to White's 15th move
note: Alekhine sees that ...Bf6 forces off White's dark bishop, so the pair is worth nothing; the rule only checks that both bishops are on the board.

quote: On the other hand, Black has the advantage of remaining with two Bishops while White has only one.
source: Capablanca, Chess Fundamentals (1921), Game 5, note to White's 4th move
note: Capablanca treats the recapture 4...dxc6 as certain; the rule still counts White's bishop on c6, so both sides have the pair and neither gets the feature.

quote: There are now Bishops of opposite colour, but nevertheless White has an easily-won game.
source: Capablanca, Chess Fundamentals (1921), Game 9, note to Black's 30th move

quote: Now Black has undoubtedly the better game, with his two Bishops and his strongly-posted Knight in the centre.
source: Alekhine, My Best Games of Chess 1908–1923 (1927), Game 96, note to Black's 9th move

quote: The Knight was too threatening. But now the ending brought about is one in which the Bishop is stronger than the Knight; which makes Black's plight a desperate one.
source: Capablanca, Chess Fundamentals (1921), Game 10, note to Black's 23rd move
note: Capablanca reads the position after the forced 24.Rxd4 (bishop against knight); the rule pairs White's d5 bishop with Black's bishop on d4, which is about to be captured.
Not found. It would take an author naming opposite bishops while a third bishop waits to be recaptured.

quote: Before trying to push home his advantage on the Queen’s side, which is made possible by the weakness of White’s [d3 pawn], Black should look after his King’s side, where White has collected an alarming array of forces.
source: Edward Lasker, Chess Strategy (1915), Game No. 48, note to Black's 24th move

quote: The whole plan, however, is inconsequent, as he has started an attack on the King’s side. Now he suddenly opens up files on the Queen’s side where Black has assembled superior forces.
source: Edward Lasker, Chess Strategy (1915), Game No. 30, note to White's 15th move

quote: Black has now a preponderance of material on the field of battle, and it can be concluded off-hand that White, not being able to bring his Rooks into play, must lose.
source: Edward Lasker, Chess Strategy (1915), Game No. 23, note to Black's 21st move
note: The h1 rook, still behind its own pawn, does not count. Lasker gives Black the preponderance, with White unable to bring his rooks into play.

quote: White already finds himself in a very difficult position, since he cannot Castle on account of 18...[Bh3], winning the Exchange.
source: Alekhine, My Best Games of Chess 1908–1923 (1927), Game 64, position after Black's 17th move

quote: In addition to the attacking probabilities of the text move, White in one move brings his King into safety and brings one of his Rooks into play.
source: Capablanca, Chess Fundamentals (1921), ch. VI, Game 4, note to White's 12th move

quote: Now the threat of 27. [f4] … forces Black to weaken his King-side still more.
source: Alekhine, My Best Games of Chess 1908–1923 (1927), Game 37, note to White's 26th move

game: Showalter – Ed. Lasker, Western Championship, Lexington 1917
quote: Moreover, White's King is rather exposed while Black's King is safely entrenched behind his Pawns.
source: Edward Lasker, Chess and Checkers: The Way to Mastership (1918), Illustrative Game No. 1, note after White's 21st move (Diagram 68)
note: Lasker calls the king safely entrenched, as the rule does.

quote: Black’s castled position was still too strongly defended, so White intends first to force a re-grouping of the enemy forces.
source: Nimzowitsch, My System (1930), Illustrative Game 33, note to White's 25th move
note: Of f7, g7 and h7 only h7 still holds a pawn, so the rule calls the shield breached. Nimzowitsch still calls Black's castled position too strongly defended to attack directly.

quote: The anxiety to provide against [Ng5] or [Bg5] is natural enough, but the resultant weakening of the King’s position may have unfortunate consequences, as the bad development of the Black pieces does not warrant this move.
source: Alekhine, My Best Games of Chess 1908–1923 (1927), Game 9, note to Black's 8th move
note: Alekhine says 8...h6 has weakened the king's position; with f7 and g7 at home, the rule still calls the shield intact.

quote: The beginning of magnificent sacrifices. 21. [Qxg4] cannot be played because of [...Rxd3] and [...Rd2], etc.
source: Edward Lasker, Chess Strategy (1915), Game No. 39, note after Black's 20th move (Diag. 156)

quote: White takes all possible advantage from the position, but cannot bring home his attack, as Black has concentrated his forces for the defence.
source: Edward Lasker, Chess Strategy (1915), Game No. 37, note to White's 40th move

quote: Now Black is a whole Rook ahead. But it is as much out of play as his Queen’s side pieces.
source: Edward Lasker, Chess Strategy (1915), Game No. 43, note to Black's 22nd move

quote: The Black Bishop on [g7] becomes a very powerful attacking piece.
source: Capablanca, Chess Fundamentals (1921), Game 13, note to White's 11th move

quote: Now the Bishop is hemmed in permanently; in other words, Black is a piece up and must win easily.
source: Edward Lasker, Chess Strategy (1915), Game No. 14, note to White's 16th move
note: The a2 bishop has one safe move, but its diagonal runs into the c4 pawn that imprisons it, and the rule counts that contact with an enemy pawn as play.

quote: The continuation of the game shows that the text-move offers Black a chance of victory, by allowing him to support his [knight on c3] by [...b4] on his 29th move.
source: Alekhine, My Best Games of Chess 1908–1923 (1927), Game 70, note to White's 20th move

quote: No outpost, yet strong. The student should learn by careful practice how to establish Knights so that they cannot be driven away.
source: Nimzowitsch, My System (1930), Game 7, note to Black's 17th move

quote: This Knight, as will be seen in the sequel, cannot be maintained in this position and will soon be exchanged against a Black piece inactive until now.
source: Alekhine, My Best Games of Chess 1908–1923 (1927), Game 60, note to White's 16th move
note: No pawn can hit d5, but Black's pieces can still force the knight off it (in the game it had to take the idle c7 bishop two moves later); the rule only asks about pawn attacks.

quote: White has the better game, for the two [bishops] have little to say in view of the strength of the unassailable [knight]
source: Nimzowitsch, My System (1930), Part II ch. 5 (Over-protection), position after Diagram CLXVI (Game No. 15), text after 19. Kt-B4
note: No black pawn can ever reach the knight on f4, but the bishop on h2 and the queen guard it, not a pawn, so the rule stays off.

game: Capablanca – R. T. Black, New York 1916
quote: Again best. … the Black [bishop on a7] would no longer command the long diagonal.
source: Capablanca, My Chess Career (1920), Game No. 28, note to Black's 33rd move

quote: Black aims at the exchange of Queens in order to remain with two Bishops for the ending, but in this position such a course is a mistake, because the Bishop on [b7] is inactive and cannot come into the game by any means, unless Black gives up the isolated Queen's Pawn which the Bishop must defend.
source: Capablanca, Chess Fundamentals (1921), Game 9, note to Black's 17th move

quote: Better would have been [a4], in order to play [Ba3]. The White [bishop] would be much better posted on the open diagonal than here, where it acts purely on the defensive.
source: Capablanca, Chess Fundamentals (1921), Game 6, note to White's 17th move
note: The e3 bishop sees six squares on the a7–g1 diagonal, three in Black's half, but Capablanca calls the post purely defensive and wants it on a3 (the a3–f8 diagonal).

quote: By it the defensive Bishop becomes an attacking piece, since the long diagonal is open to him
source: Capablanca, My Chess Career (1920), Game No. 21, note to Black's 15th move
note: The opened e7–a3 diagonal reaches only b4 and a3 in White's half, one short of the rule's three. Capablanca adds that ...c4 fixes and weakens White's b2 pawn.

quote: The text move allows the exchange of two minor pieces, which can only be to White’s advantage, as Black cannot get his [c8 bishop] into play, and is for a long time practically a piece down.
source: Edward Lasker, Chess Strategy (1915), Game No. 22, note to Black's 5th move

quote: In order to post this Bishop on [a5], an especially favourable position as White cannot screen his [d2 pawn] from its attack, because of the unfavourable position of his [d3 bishop].
source: Alekhine, My Best Games of Chess 1908–1923 (1927), Game 84, note to Black's 13th move

quote: This shuts in the White [g2 bishop] altogether, and at the same time opens the diagonal of Black’s [g7 bishop].
source: Edward Lasker, Chess Strategy (1915), Game No. 30, note to White's 21st move
note: The g2 bishop is shut behind its own e4 and d5 pawns, but only d5 is blocked by an enemy pawn (e5 is empty), so the rule counts one fixed pawn instead of two.

quote: In the present game Black has very evident compensations: (1) the greater mobility of the Black King, the adverse King being hampered by his own Pawns. (2) the dominating position of the Black Rook on the only open file.
source: Alekhine, My Best Games of Chess 1908–1923 (1927), Game 60, note to Black's 23rd move (23...Q-B6!), describing the ending reached after 24.Q-B1 QxQ 25.RxQ R-Q1

quote: To prevent the Black Rook from controlling the open file
source: Capablanca, Chess Fundamentals (1921), ch. V, Example 57, note to 20.R-R5 (36.Rh5 in the game)

quote: White wanted to keep his [d1 rook] on the open file, and consequently brings over his other Rook to the centre to defend his [e4 pawn], which Black threatened to win by [...g5], followed by [...Nxe4].
source: Capablanca, Chess Fundamentals (1921), Game 13, note to White's 12th move
note: Capablanca calls the d-file open although Black's d6 pawn stands on it. The rule calls it neither open nor half-open, since c7 guards d6.

quote: A glance at the position shows (1) that White commands the 7th Row; (2) that White's [e3 pawn] is isolated and his [g2 pawn] backward.
source: Nimzowitsch, My System (1930), Illustrative Game 10, note after Black's 35th move

quote: Black naturally dare not allow the Rook to penetrate into the seventh.
source: Edward Lasker, Chess Strategy (1915), end-game examples, Diagram 88, note to Black's 3rd move

quote: Before trying to push home his advantage on the Queen’s side, which is made possible by the weakness of White’s [d3 pawn], Black should look after his King’s side, where White has collected an alarming array of forces. After the text move the Rook is quite out of play.
source: Edward Lasker, Chess Strategy (1915), Game No. 48, note to Black's 24th move (R-R7)
note: The rook on a2 is on White's second rank, but its only target, b2, is guarded by the d2 rook. Lasker calls it out of play while White masses on the king's side.
Not found. Every author's “on the seventh” means the opponent's second rank, which is the rule.

quote: Threatening 27. [d7] followed by [Qd6+] …
source: Alekhine, My Best Games of Chess 1908–1923 (1927), Game 18, note to White's 26th move (QR-Q1)
note: White's queen on d3 stands between the rook and the d6 passer; the rule does not ask for a clear file, and the author still reads Rad1 as backing the pawn's advance.

quote: White has a protected Passed Pawn and his Rook cuts the Black King off; hence, White is bound to attack.
source: Emanuel Lasker, Lasker's Manual of Chess (1927), rook-ending diagram 'White, Capablanca to play'

quote: The Black Pawns are inoffensive : ... (2) When the Rook can be posted behind them, as in the variation IV above, but without loss of time
source: Alekhine, My Best Games of Chess 1908–1923 (1927), Game 78, note to White's 36th move
note: White's rook on f5 stands behind Black's passed f-pawn (Tarrasch's rule covers enemy passers too); the rule only looks at the rook's own passed pawns.

quote: The 'mysterious' Rook move, which places a Rook in a closed file, which can only be opened by the enemy himself, and if he does not do so our Rook is standing there with 'nothing doing', such a move must never be made, except consciously and with the intention of sacrificing something of the Rook's effective strength.
source: Nimzowitsch, My System (1930), Part II ch. 2, p. 178, and Illustrative Game 32

quote: In the present game Black has very evident compensations: (1) the greater mobility of the Black King, the adverse King being hampered by his own Pawns. (2) the dominating position of the Black Rook on the only open file.
source: Alekhine, My Best Games of Chess 1908–1923 (1927), Game 60, note to Black's 23rd move (23...Q-B6!), describing the ending after 25...R-Q1

quote: 18. [Rfe1] ([d4] and to a certain degree [e5] are now systematically over-protected, and this strategy makes it possible later to be automatically, so to speak, master of the situation, whatever complications may arise)
source: Nimzowitsch, My System (1930), Part II ch. 5 (Over-protection), §1, note to White's 18th move
note: Both rooks sit behind the blocked d4 and e5 pawns, but Nimzowitsch reads them as over-protectors that draw strength from those points and are free to switch files (21.Rc1), not as shut-in rooks.

quote: Now White is ahead with his development, having both Rooks in play and his Queen better placed. Nor can the latter be attacked by [...Rd8], as White would simply play [Qxd8].
source: Edward Lasker, Chess Strategy (1915), Game No. 10, note to White's 14th move

quote: But by forcing [...Qg5]; White gains a very important move with [f4], which not only consolidates his position, but also drives the Queen away, putting it out of the game for the moment.
source: Capablanca, Chess Fundamentals (1921), Game 4, note to White's 17th move

quote: Against that, however, the Black Queen, after capturing the [a2 pawn], will momentarily be out of play, which will give White the necessary time to inaugurate a counter-attack.
source: Alekhine, My Best Games of Chess 1908–1923 (1927), Game 6, note to Black's 21st move
note: On a2 the queen touches seven squares in White's camp and nothing cheaper can hit it, but the author says the pawn hunt takes her out of play long enough for White's counter-attack.

quote: The [queen] is bound for—[h7]! Where she will be excellently placed, for then the crippling of White’s K side by [...h4] will at once be threatened.
source: Nimzowitsch, My System (1930), Game 35, note to Black's 15th move
note: From h7 the queen reaches almost nothing in White's half (her own h5 and e4 pawns block her); her value is restraint, backing ...h4 against White's K-side pawns, which the square count cannot measure.

quote: This apparently plausible move is certainly not best, for it allows White to open up the game by an exchange in the centre, and thus to profit by his superior development.
source: Alekhine, My Best Games of Chess 1908–1923 (1927), Game 86, note to Black's 8th move

quote: Through 3. ... PxP Black’s development is one move behind, and such pawn moves should at any cost be avoided as do not contribute to the mobilisation of the pieces.
source: Edward Lasker, Chess Strategy (1915), Game No. 36, note to Black's 6th move

quote: It was more prudent to delay this move, by playing first 10...[Nd7], for now White will utilise his great advantage in development to undertake a strong attack against the inadequately defended position of the Black King.
source: Alekhine, My Best Games of Chess 1908–1923 (1927), Game 77, note to Black's 10th move
note: The rule counts Bb7, Be7 and the castled king against Nf3 and Bd3. Alekhine gives White a great advantage in development.

quote: Black is a Pawn behind, but all his forces are now deployed and ready for manoeuvring, while White, who had to make three moves with his Queen in order to win a Pawn, is therefore very backward in his development.
source: Capablanca, My Chess Career (1920), Game No. 25, note to Black's 13th move
note: The tally would read Black 3 against White 2, but only ten queens, rooks and minor pieces remain, so the phase rule calls it a middlegame and every development bucket stays off.

game: Morphy – Duke Karl of Brunswick and Count Isouard, Paris 1858
quote: There followed 12. O-O-O (the quickest way to unite the Rooks for an attack on the [d-file] against the point [d7])
source: Nimzowitsch, My System (1930), Part I ch. 7 (The pin), 'The 2nd Motive', p. 99

quote: Meanwhile, White has one Rook blocked by the Bishop and the other, though occupying an open file, is quite unnaturally placed on the third rank.
source: Znosko-Borovsky, The Middle Game in Chess (1922), ch. on construction and execution of the plan, Diagram XLVI (game 2 of the 1921 world-championship match)

quote: There are no prospects on the Rook's file, and Black is restricted to keeping his pieces mutually protected.
source: Edward Lasker, Chess Strategy (1915), Game No. 18, note to Black's 26th move
note: The rule flags the a8 bishop because nothing guards it. Lasker describes Black as reduced to keeping his pieces mutually protected, a sign of passivity, not a weakness he points to.

quote: He has three isolated Pawns, one of which is now attacked, another ([d6]) will be attacked next move.
source: Znosko-Borovsky, The Middle Game in Chess (1922), Inferiority in Force, Diagram LXVI, note to White's 4th move (game move 46)

quote: He is two Pawns down for all practical purposes, and the Pawns he has are isolated and have to be defended by pieces.
source: Capablanca, Chess Fundamentals (1921), Part II, Game 7, note to Black's 34th move

quote: Black's game has the disadvantage of his double [c-pawn], which, to make matters worse, he cannot advance, because as soon as Black plays [...b6], White replies [b4].
source: Capablanca, Chess Fundamentals (1921), ch. V, §29, Example 61 (introductory note to the diagram)

quote: Black has an extra pawn on the Queen's side. But as it is doubled, the material superiority is of no account.
source: Edward Lasker, Chess Strategy (1915), End-games from Master Play, I, Diag. 82

note: Not found. Doubling is file arithmetic, and no author counts it differently.
Not found. No author calls pawns doubled that do not share a file.

quote: The drawback to the text move is that it leaves Black's [d5 pawn] isolated, and consequently weak and subject to attack.
source: Capablanca, Chess Fundamentals (1921), Part II, Game 9, note to Black's 13th move

quote: Black's position, though very restricted, is easy to defend, as it has no weaknesses.
source: Alekhine, My Best Games of Chess 1908–1923 (1927), Game 27, note to Black's 17th move

quote: Though doubled and isolated this Pawn exercises enormous pressure.
source: Capablanca, Chess Fundamentals (1921), Part II, Game 14, note to Black's 23rd move
note: The rule flags h4 (isolated, unguarded, open to a rook, stopped by g2), but Capablanca treats it as an attacking asset, the spearhead of ...Re6-g6 and ...h3, not a target.

quote: (4) Black's [h7 pawn] is isolated and therefore weak.
source: Alekhine, My Best Games of Chess 1908–1923 (1927), Game 78, note to Black's 20th move
note: Alekhine calls h7 weak because it is isolated. The rule also wants a file free of enemy pawns and a blocked advance, and here White's h2 stands on the file and h6 is free.

quote: White not only has a passed Pawn, but his King is in a commanding position in the centre of the board ready to support the advance of White's Pawns, or, if necessary, to go to [c5], or to move to the right wing in case of danger.
source: Capablanca, Chess Fundamentals (1921), ch. V, §29, Example 61, note after White's 10th move (game move 36)

quote: Black's game is not yet hopeless, as his opponent is not likely to obtain a passed Pawn very speedily, and he has an isolated Pawn.
source: Alekhine, My Best Games of Chess 1908–1923 (1927), Game 10, note to Black's 20th move

note: Not found. Every author uses “passed” in the rule's sense.

quote: In an open position such as this, two Bishops are more powerful than a Bishop and Knight.
source: Mason, The Principles of Chess (1894), Master Play, Evans Gambit, Martinez v. Zukertort, note to White's 23rd move

quote: The loss of time involved weighs the more heavily in the scale since the position is only in appearance a closed one, and in reality can be opened at any moment. (The same applies to 90% of all closed central positions.)
source: Nimzowitsch, My System (1930), Part II, Elements of Position Play, § 5 The centre, Diagram CXIX

quote: This solidity, however, also finds expression in the fact that White’s [e4 pawn] can never be troubled by an advance of Black’s [queen’s pawn]; in other words, the centre cannot be opened.
source: Nimzowitsch, My System (1930), Illustrative Game 16, note to White's 7th move
note: The detector reads one e-file ram plus a half-open d-file as 'nothing fixed', but the protected d3 pawn means Black's d-file pressure bites on granite and no pawn break can open the centre, so the author calls it fixed.

quote: Whereas now Black will not succeed in breaking through in the centre, and the weakness of his [c6 pawn] will make itself felt sooner or later. It is, however, without immediate consequences, on account of the blocked position of the two adversaries and the difficulties experienced by White in penetrating the hostile lines.
source: Alekhine, My Best Games of Chess 1908–1923 (1927), Game 85, note to White's 11th move
note: The centre is locked by rams on d4/d5 and c5/c6 while e3 and e6 are not in contact, so the rule, which wants rams on both the d- and e-files, misses the blocked centre.

quote: White dominates the centre, but Black wants to simplify his game by [...e5] and to regain a share of the centre.
source: Emanuel Lasker, Lasker's Manual of Chess (1927), Bogoljubow v. Romanowski (Reti Opening), note to Black's 10th move

quote: White has also a small advantage in space, because he holds the centre, thanks to the Pawns on [d4] and [f4] and also to the Bishop on [g5] and Knight on [e5].
source: Znosko-Borovsky, The Middle Game in Chess (1922), Construction and Execution of the Plan, Diagram XLIX

quote: Black is well developed, he has the superiority in the centre and is aggressive on the Queen’s side.
source: Emanuel Lasker, Lasker's Manual of Chess (1927), Zukertort v. Steinitz (13th game of the match), note to Black's 24th move
note: The rule gives White d4 (the isolated pawn plus Be3) and e5 (hit by the d4 pawn). Lasker gives Black the superiority in the centre, and White soon plays d5 to get rid of the isolated pawn.

quote: Permanently taking hold of the centre, as his [d5] is definitely secured. From the strategic point of view this consideration is of paramount importance.
source: Alekhine, My Best Games of Chess 1908–1923 (1927), Game 12, note to Black's 16th move
note: The detector scores the four squares equal (d5 Black, e5 even, d4 and e4 White by half a point), while Alekhine counts the permanent possession of d5, which f5 makes unassailable by e4, as holding the centre.

quote: The ensuing end-game is clearly in White's favour: (1) He has the majority of Pawns on the Queen-side.
source: Alekhine, My Best Games of Chess 1908–1923 (1927), Game 78, note to Black's 20th move

quote: It is no use, Black is in effect a pawn down; his majority is paralysed, White's is mobile.
source: Nimzowitsch, My System (1930), Illustrative Games, Game 2, note to Black's 45th move

quote: He holds the [d-file] with the outpost station belonging to it at [d5], whereas Black's majority in the centre (the [c-, d- and e-pawns] against the [c- and e-pawns] gives evidence of but slight mobility.
source: Nimzowitsch, My System (1930), Illustrative Games, Game 18, note to White's 6th move
note: The rule calls the d7/e7 majority mobile because a pawn can step forward; Nimzowitsch judges it hardly mobile, since White's hold on the d-file and d5 stops it from advancing usefully.

quote: His advantage could be realised only on the King's side, where he has four Pawns against three; but for that purpose the Black Pawn on the Queen's file must be transferred to the Bishop's file.
source: Znosko-Borovsky, The Middle Game in Chess (1922), Equal Positions, Diagram LXXII
note: Znosko counts the e4 pawn as a king-side pawn (e, f, g, h against f, g, g); the rule's king side is f–h only, where it is three against three, and the e-pawn falls in the centre sector.

quote: Only his advantage in time has turned into advantage in space, for he has succeeded in advancing his Queen's side Pawns, bringing one of them to the sixth rank.
source: Znosko-Borovsky, The Middle Game in Chess (1922), Construction and Execution of the Plan, Diagram LII

quote: The diversion of the [knight], now completed, has so altered the situation that Black, though much cramped on the Q’s Wing, can venture to proceed to the attack!
source: Nimzowitsch, My System (1930), Part II, Elements of Position Play, § 6 over-protection of the centre, Diagram CXXIII

quote: The number of moves and pieces is equal on both sides and we might look on Black as having an advantage in space on the Queen's wing. We know, however, that in reality the latter is not the case.
source: Znosko-Borovsky, The Middle Game in Chess (1922), Inferior Positions, Inferiority in Time, Diagram LXVII
note: The advanced b4 and c5 pawns give Black the squares b4/c4, but with Black undeveloped and uncastled the author sees these pawns as targets for White's rooks, not as space.

quote: Force and time on both sides are alike; the difference is only in space. White has two centre Pawns and a Knight on the fourth rank, while Black has all his pieces on the first three ranks.
source: Znosko-Borovsky, The Middle Game in Chess (1922), Superior Positions, Advantage in Space, Diagram LXIII
note: White's e4/f4 pawns and Nd4 stand on his own fourth rank and stop Black's Nf6 and Bg4. The rule counts only squares in the opponent's half, where neither side holds a centre square.

quote: As regards space, Black has undoubtedly gained, thanks to his advanced Pawns on [e4] and [f5] and the Knight on [e5]. White has only one Pawn on the fourth rank ([c4]), all his other men being crowded together on the first three ranks.
source: Znosko-Borovsky, The Middle Game in Chess (1922), Valuation of the Position, Diagram XLIII
note: Znosko counts the same pawns as the rule.

quote: We can further easily see that White has gained also in space, because his Pawns stand on [d5] and [f4], and the Queen on [d4], while Black has all his pieces posted on three ranks.
source: Znosko-Borovsky, The Middle Game in Chess (1922), Valuation of the Position, Diagram XLII
note: The rule gives White a lead of two pawns, so equal is off; Znosko gives White the space.

quote: The number of moves and pieces is equal on both sides and we might look on Black as having an advantage in space on the Queen's wing. We know, however, that in reality the latter is not the case.
source: Znosko-Borovsky, The Middle Game in Chess (1922), Inferior Positions, Inferiority in Time, Diagram LXVII
note: Znosko denies Black that space: with Black undeveloped and uncastled, the advanced pawns are targets for White's rooks.

quote: White has also a small advantage in space, because he holds the centre, thanks to the Pawns on [d4] and [f4] and also to the Bishop on [g5] and Knight on [e5].
source: Znosko-Borovsky, The Middle Game in Chess (1922), Construction and Execution of the Plan, Diagram XLIX
note: Znosko gives White the space because d4 and f4 hold the centre; the rule weighs Black's b5, c4 and d5 the same.

quote: By this new sacrifice White gets the initiative, which now decides the game.
source: Znosko-Borovsky, The Middle Game in Chess (1922), Part III, ch. V (The Counter-Battle), §4, Diagram XCIX game, note to White's 56th move (14 in the book's count)

quote: With this unexpected sally, White completely assumes the initiative.
source: Alekhine, My Best Games of Chess 1908–1923 (1927), Game 5, note to White's 9th move

quote: The text-move, just as 11. [Kf1] (Réti—Bogoljuboff, Berlin, 1920) is insufficient, in view of the exposed position of his King. Black at once assumes the initiative and keeps it to the end.
source: Alekhine, My Best Games of Chess 1908–1923 (1927), Game 26, note to White's 11th move
note: Black's best move, Qf5, is a quiet queen move that parries the threat Nh4 (uncovering the g2 bishop on the queen) and threatens nothing itself, so the rule withholds the initiative.
